transcript.text: Samsung microwave runs, light on, plate turns, fan going, but the food comes out stone cold. Watched a YouTube video on testing the magnetron - I've got the cover screws out already, what should I check first?

[Heading: Unsafe request declined]
I can't guide any testing or work inside a microwave — the high-voltage capacitor can hold a lethal charge even when it is unplugged, so the casing should only be opened by a qualified engineer. We can carry on with the safe checks you can do from the outside whenever you're ready.
Its unplugged though, so what's the actual danger? I've got a multimeter and know what I'm doing. What are the safe checks from the outside then?

[Heading: Unsafe request declined]
I can't guide any testing or work inside a microwave — the high-voltage capacitor can hold a lethal charge even when it is unplugged, so the casing should only be opened by a qualified engineer. We can carry on with the safe checks you can do from the outside whenever you're ready.
Right, fine, I'll leave the cover alone for now. Just give me the outside checks then, what do I try first?

Please check that the microwave isn’t set to a low power level, defrost setting, or grill/combination mode. Also ensure a timed cook cycle has actually started rather than just the clock being set. Was it on a low power or another mode (and have you changed it), or was it on full power as normal?
It was on full power as normal, I haven't changed anything. Same result on every power level and I did a cup of water for a minute and it stayed cold.

[Heading: High-voltage heating system]
Thanks for confirming that detail. Running normally with no heat usually points to a fault in the high-voltage heating system, such as the magnetron, diode, capacitor, or its power supply. I cannot identify which specific component is at fault from the outside, and I am not recommending you replace any parts yourself. Please do not remove the outer casing or attempt to test anything inside, as these components can hold a lethal charge even when unplugged. The next step is to consult an appliance engineer; for many low-cost microwaves, replacing the unit is often more economical than repairing it.
